newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Odds stacked on May 1-3 '98 for EMU entry decision.
newsitem.headline: Odds stacked on May 1-3 '98 for EMU entry decision.

text.p: European Union finance ministers stopped short on Saturday of giving firm dates for a final decision on who qualifies for the launch of European monetary union, but indicated this was little more than a year away.
A number of thinly-veiled hints, following an informal meeting between them, pointed to the long weekend of May 1-3, 1998 as the most likely timing.
The ministers agreed at the meeting that the crucial decision would be taken over an extended weekend session in late April or early May of next year.
Irish finance minister Ruairi Quinn said the decisive meeting would kick off one Friday with a gathering of ECOFIN -- the EU's finance ministers and central bankers.
Talks would continue on the Saturday in the form of a special summit of European Union heads of government, and ECOFIN would resume talks on the Sunday.
The three-day session would establish which countries will meld their currencies into the euro in 1999, and set up the operating basis for the European Central Bank, he added.
Quinn, like other European finance ministers, declined to comment specifically on when the meeting would be held.
But asked by a journalist whether the talks would take place "on a bank holiday weekend", Quinn replied "For some people".
May 1 is a public holiday in most of Europe but not in the United Kingdom, which will have the EU presidency at the time, or in Ireland.
Taking such a decision on a day when many financial markets are closed would be of significant advantage, given the potential impact the decisions could have on currency markets.
Separately, Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt, asked to comment on the likelihood of those dates, remarked: "Just look in your diaries".
Countries which wish to qualify for EMU should meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget deficits and public debt laid down in the Maastricht Treaty in 1997.

Although the European Union called at its 1995 Madrid summit for a decision on entrants to monetary union to take place as soon as possible in 1998, ministers said that this would not be realistic before late April at the earliest.
As the toughest target for most is on budget deficits, it will be essential to have accurate budget results for 1997 available before a decision can be made.

Once these have been presented, in late February, both the European Commission and European Monetary Institute -- the forerunner to the European Central Bank -- will draw up reports giving their views on who qualifies for EMU.

After a further meeting of the EU finance ministers, at which they will make recommendations, the issue will need to be considered by the European parliament, and the relevant national parliaments, before the final decision can be made.

Dutch finance minister Gerrit Zalm, who chaired Saturday's talks, told reporters that etiquette related to the parliamentary consultations was one key reason why no date for the decision-making meeting had been formally set here.

"We were not able to fix an exact date because we are dependent on the European parliament," he said, adding that setting a date would place a limit on the length of the European parliament's debate on the issue.
"It is not elegant to do that," he said.
